## Round 2: System Design & DSA Deep Dive

> Duration: 1 Hour   
> Interviewer: Associate (SDE2)

This round began with a deep dive into my resume, specifically my work at AWS. She asked me to sketch out the **Low-Level Design (LLD)** and scalability architecture of my project.

* **Discussion:** We discussed configuring reverse proxies, adding load balancers, implementing “LLM rerouters,” and orchestrating agents in production.

Once she was satisfied with my design skills, we moved to DSA:

1. [**Asteroid Collision**](https://leetcode.com/problems/asteroid-collision/)**:** She asked me to code and explain simultaneously. I used a **Stack-based approach** and proactively walked her through edge cases (e.g., asteroids of equal size colliding).
2. [**Trapping Rain Water**](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/trapping-rain-water/)**:** A classic hard problem. I initially coded a Dynamic Programming solution. She asked for an optimization to **O(1) space and one pass**. I quickly refactored it using the two-pointer approach.

**Outcome:** She appreciated my design and project skills, and I was shifted to the second waiting room.

## Round 3: Advanced Algo & OOPs

> Duration: 1 Hour 20 Minutes  
> Time: 3:30 PM  
> Interviewer: Associate (SDE3)

This was arguably the toughest round. The interviewer wasted no time and jumped straight into a complex **Low-Level Design** problem.

* **The Task:** I was given an abstract problem statement and had to draw the **UML diagram**, define class entities, and apply design patterns (Factory/Strategy) on the whiteboard. This lasted about 15 minutes.
* **Rapid Fire:** Immediately after, he grilled me on Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs) nuances and database scaling strategies.

**The DSA Challenge:**

* **Problem:** [**Repeated String Match**](https://leetcode.com/problems/repeated-string-match/)
* **Approach:** I started with a Brute Force solution. He wasn’t satisfied and pushed for optimization. I implemented the **KMP Search** algorithm. As a follow-up for further optimization, he asked for the **Rabin-Karp** (Rolling Hash) approach.

Goldman Sachs Summer Analyst Internship Interview Experience 2025 (Selected)
Hi everyone,
I recently went through the Goldman Sachs Summer Analyst internship hiring process and wanted to share my experience. Hopefully, this helps anyone preparing for it!


---


Online Assessment (1 hour)
Multiple MCQs + 3 coding problems + 1 situation-based essay.
Topics: DSA, OOPs, and some basic math.

---



Interview Process (3 eliminatory rounds)

Round 1 (Technical)
Discussion about one of the projects from my resume.
DSA Question: Rotten Oranges variation (fruits instead). Given a test case and asked to dry run it.
Follow-ups and discussed edge cases.

Round 2 (Technical + HR)
Again discussed a project from my resume.
HR: Challenges faced while doing the project.
The interviewer gave a case and asked how I would implement that scenario in my project (follow-up question).
DSA Question: Given two strings s and p, find all starting indices of anagrams of p in s.
JavaScript questions were linked to the DSA problem — for example, how I would implement the logic and handle the results on the frontend for this DSA question.
Follow-ups, discussed edge cases, and time complexity.

Round 3 (Technical)
Discussion about one of the projects from my resume.
DSA Question: Given currency conversion rates, determine if there exists a conversion path that can yield a profit.

Each round lasted ~30-40 minutes.

Verdict: Selected 🎉

## Technical Round 3:

I anxiously awaited, refreshing my inbox every ten minutes in anticipation of the HR email signaling the third round. When it finally arrived a day before my interview, it felt like a weight had been lifted off my shoulders. Little did I realize at the time, the challenges that awaited me in what would turn out to be a less-than-ideal interview experience. My interviewer did not introduce himself and went straight into the interview. He asked me why I wanted to join GS. Then he gave a sort of system design question where I had to build a system that would calculate the number of people in the building at each time so that we can access the amount of resources that will be required. I started explaining that from security logins at the gate, I could get the number of people present and so on. The questions progressed from my answer itself going into memory allocation in a computer and how to take the smallest amount of memory space for this task. The questions were more on storage efficiency. I was able to answer, but I did get nervous as this wasn’t something I was prepared for. After the interview, I made a note to myself that I need to be more confident in my learnings. This did leave me a little confused about my further chances.

## Technical Interview 4:

A week after the third round, I received a call from the HR regarding the fourth round, which was scheduled for the next day. As my end-semester exams were ongoing, I had to divide my time in order to prepare for both. From 10–12 noon, I had my end-semester exam, and my interview was scheduled at 12:15 pm. After the exam, I rushed back to my room, changed into formals, and revised from my short notes.

My interview started with a brief introduction, followed by some questions from my resume regarding my internship. The interviewer was impressed as I had completed my research internship at IIT BHU, and I explained to him my work in creating a morphological dictionary of a regional language. Then, I was given a DSA question — *Longest common substring*. I was able to code it and then provide its optimized version using tabulation. He then asked me to create the DP table using an example, and using my code, I was able to create the entire DP table for the given example.
